title: Κύων ⟨ἑστιώμενος.⟩ siue Ἄνθρωπος καὶ κύων
titleEn: The Dog at the Feast, or The Man and the Dog
part: The Dog at the Feast, or The Man and the Dog (Chambry 178)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 178. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἄνθρωπός τις ἡτοίμαζε δεῖπνον, ἑστιάσων τινὰ τῶν φίλων αὐτῷ καὶ οἰκείων.
sentences.tr: Anthrōpos tis hētoimaze deipnon, hestiasōn tina tōn philōn autōi kai oikeiōn.
sentences.l: A certain man was making a dinner ready, meaning to entertain one of those dear to him and of his household.
sentences.i: A man was getting a dinner ready, meaning to entertain one of his friends and kinsmen.
sentences.n: ἑστιάσων is a future participle of purpose, "with a view to entertaining". φίλος takes the dative of the person to whom one is dear, hence τῶν φίλων αὐτῷ. οἰκεῖοι are those of the same house, and so kin.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ κύων αὐτοῦ ἄλλον κύνα ἐκάλει, λέγων· « Ὦ φίλε, δεῦρο συνδείπνησόν μοι. »
sentences.tr: Ho de kyōn autou allon kyna ekalei, legōn· « Ō phile, deuro syndeipnēson moi. »
sentences.l: And his dog was inviting another dog, saying: « Friend, come here, dine with me. »
sentences.n: καλέω is the ordinary word for inviting a man to dinner. δεῦρο is "here!", a summons that regularly stands beside an imperative. συνδειπνέω takes the dative of the one dined with.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ προσελθὼν χαίρων ἵστατο, βλέπων τὸ μέγα δεῖπνον, βοῶν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ· « Βαβαί, πόση μοι χαρὰ ἄρτι ἐξαπιναίως ἐφάνη· τραφήσομαί τε γὰρ καὶ εἰς κόρον δειπνήσω, ὥστε με αὔριον μηδαμῇ γε πεινᾶσαι. »
sentences.tr: Ho de proselthōn chairōn histato, blepōn to mega deipnon, boōn en tēi kardiāi· « Babai, posē moi chara arti exapinaiōs ephanē· traphēsomai te gar kai eis koron deipnēsō, hōste me aurion mēdamēi ge peinasai. »
sentences.l: And he, having come up, stood there rejoicing, looking at the great dinner, crying out in his heart: « Aha, what great joy has just now appeared to me all at once! For I shall both be fed and dine to my fill, so that tomorrow I shall not be hungry in any way at all. »
sentences.i: The other came and stood there delighted, gazing at the great dinner and crying out inwardly: « Aha, what joy has come to me all at once! I shall be fed and eat my fill, so that tomorrow I shall not be hungry at all. »
sentences.n: Βαβαί is a cry of astonishment, and πόση with no verb is the exclamation "how great!". τραφήσομαι is the future passive of τρέφω, "I shall be fed", paired with δειπνήσω by τε … καί. ὥστε with accusative and infinitive states the result as one looked for. εἰς κόρον is "up to satiety"; the γε in μηδαμῇ γε presses the denial.

sentences.t: Ταῦτα καθ’ ἑαυτὸν λέγοντος τοῦ κυνὸς καὶ ἅμα σείοντος τὴν κέρκον, ὡς δὴ εἰς τὸν φίλον θαρροῦντος, ὁ μάγειρος, ὡς εἶδε τοῦτον ὧδε κἀκεῖσε τὴν κέρκον περιστρέφοντα, κατασχὼν τὰ σκέλη αὐτοῦ ἔρριψε παραχρῆμα ἔξωθεν τῶν θυρίδων.
sentences.tr: Tauta kath’ heauton legontos tou kynos kai hama seiontos tēn kerkon, hōs dē eis ton philon tharrountos, ho mageiros, hōs eide touton hōde kakeise tēn kerkon peristrephonta, kataschōn ta skelē autou erripse parachrēma exōthen tōn thyridōn.
sentences.l: While the dog was saying this to himself and at the same time wagging his tail, as one trusting in his friend, the cook, when he saw him swinging his tail this way and that, took hold of his legs and threw him then and there outside the windows.
sentences.i: As the dog said this to himself, wagging his tail all the while in his confidence toward his friend, the cook saw him whipping his tail this way and that, caught him by the legs, and pitched him straight out of the window.
sentences.n: A long genitive absolute (λέγοντος … σείοντος … θαρροῦντος) runs on before the main clause. ὡς δή with a participle gives the reason as the dog himself saw it, not as the narrator vouches for it. θαρρέω εἰς is to have one's confidence directed toward someone. κἀκεῖσε is crasis for καὶ ἐκεῖσε. ἡ θυρίς is the small window set high in a wall; the plural here is general, and the idiomatic line puts it in the singular.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ κατιὼν ἀπῄει μεγάλως κράζων.
sentences.tr: Ho de katiōn apēiei megalōs krazōn.
sentences.l: And he, going down, went off crying loudly.

sentences.t: Τῶν τις δὲ κυνῶν, τῶν καθ’ ὁδὸν αὐτῷ σαναντώντων, ἐπηρώτα· « Πῶς ἐδείπνησας, φίλος ; »
sentences.tr: Tōn tis de kynōn, tōn kath’ hodon autōi sanantōntōn, epērōta· « Pōs edeipnēsas, philos ; »
sentences.l: And one of the dogs, of those meeting him along the road, asked: « How did you dine, friend? »
sentences.i: And one of the dogs he met along the road asked him: « How was your dinner, friend? »
sentences.n: σαναντώντων is what the page prints; the word wanted is συναντώντων, "meeting" with the dative αὐτῷ, and this looks like a slip of the press rather than a reading — but the text is given as printed. φίλος is a nominative doing the work of a vocative, as often in easy speech. Chambry sets a space before the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν ὑπολαβὼν ἔφη· « Ἐκ τῆς πολλῆς πόσεως μεθυσθεὶς ὑπὲρ κόρον οὐδὲ τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτὴν ὅθεν ἐξῆλθον οἶδα. »
sentences.tr: Ho de pros auton hypolabōn ephē· « Ek tēs pollēs poseōs methystheis hyper koron oude tēn hodon autēn hothen exēlthon oida. »
sentences.l: And he, taking-up-the-word to him, said: « Made drunk beyond satiety by all that drinking, I do not so much as know the road itself by which I came out. »
sentences.i: And he took up the word and said: « Drunk beyond satiety with all that drinking, I do not even know the road I came out by. »
sentences.n: ὑπολαβών is the same idiom as ὑποτυχών, taking up another's word to answer it. ὑπὲρ κόρον, "beyond satiety", answers the εἰς κόρον he had promised himself. ὅθεν, "whence", hangs loosely on τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτήν. He keeps his boast and tells the truth in the same breath.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οὐ δεῖ θαρρεῖν τοῖς ἐξ ἀλλοτρίων εὖ ποιεῖν ἐπαγγελλομένοις.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ou dei tharrein tois ex allotriōn eu poiein epangellomenois.
sentences.l: The fable shows that one must not trust those who promise to do good out of what belongs to others.
sentences.n: θαρρέω with the dative is to put one's confidence in a person. ἐξ ἀλλοτρίων is "out of other men's goods". ἐπαγγέλλομαι is to profess or promise publicly, and takes the infinitive of what is promised.
